title: What Makes the Northern Lights Glow
post_title: What Makes the Northern Lights Glow | QuantaTale
post_description: How the solar wind, Earth's magnetic shield and atmospheric gases create auroras, from NASA and NOAA. Sources: National Aeronautics and Space Administration https://science.nasa.gov/sun/auroras/ and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/news/science-beauty-and-mystery-auroras #Science #ScienceFacts #QuantaTale
narration: What makes the sky glow green near the poles? The Sun constantly sends out charged particles called the solar wind. At Earth, energy builds up in the magnetic shield, and when it is released, much of it rains down on the atmosphere. In the polar regions, electrons collide with oxygen and nitrogen atoms in the upper atmosphere, and those atoms emit light. The most common colour is green, from oxygen up high. The colour depends on which gas is hit and where it sits: nitrogen glows blue, and oxygen far higher up glows red. Near the poles, auroras show up on many nights of the year. Every twist of a northern auroral ribbon is matched by a southern companion, though not in a perfect mirror image.
